new_statements.rule_in_words: King states only that stress is non-contrastive (predictable) and that /o/ and /a/ neutralize to [ʌ] in pre-stressed position; the placement itself is not stated in the scanned pages, but every polysyllabic phonetic form he transcribes on pp. 98-101 (about 45 items, e.g. ['payʌu] 'deer', [mʌm'panau] 'walk', [tu'mʌyʌg] 'swim', [nə'sirʌ] 'they', [si'suna] 'just now', [ʌ'mutan]) is stressed on the penultimate syllable, including affixed forms, so the provisional rule is: stress on the penultimate syllable of the (affixed) word, non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the scanned pages; no secondary-stress marks in transcriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Forms with vowel sequences ([ʌ'luʌm] 'soft', [lʌ'laiŋ] 'child', [sʌn'diaŋ] 'different') are consistent with penult stress if each vowel is a syllable nucleus. The explicit stress/syllable section, if any, would be on pp. 102-106, which the Rosetta scan does not include.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonemic description of isolated words, phonetic transcriptions of citation forms); Sugut-river dialect of Tombonuwo (villages Sungai-Sungai and Lingkabau, Labuk-Sugut District), data 1983.
new_statements.identity_note: King 1993 describes the Sugut-river dialect of Tombonuwo (villages Sungai-Sungai and Lingkabau, Labuk-Sugut District; Lingkabau is listed as a dialect of tomb1244 by Glottolog/Ethnologue), i.e. tomb1244 proper; King uses 'Tombonuwo' rather than 'Sungai' to keep it distinct from other 'Sungai' groups (Abai Sungai etc., which are separate Paitanic languages). The Wikipedia summary and Abdul Hamid Ahmad's 'bahasa Sungai' may not be the same variety.

new_statements.quote: ... Sungai boleh diramal secara fonemik. Hal ini berlaku demikian kerana lazimnya tekanan wujud pada suku kata praakhir dalam kata fonologi yang ditandai nada yang meninggi serta mempunyai darjah kelantangan. Walau bagaimanapun, apabila suku kata praakhir mengandungi vokal kedua daripada gugusan vokal homorganik, tekanan berubah kepada suku kata ketiga. [...] Perkataan satu suku kata dalam bahasa Sungai jarang ber-laku tetapi menghasilkan tekanan. [...] ... tekanan sering berubah kedudukannya kerana perkara-perkara yang hendak ditegaskan diberi tekanan. Dalam bahasa Sungai penekanan perkataan sering wujud pada suku kata akhir dalam frasa. (Google Books search snippets, scanned spacing before punctuation normalised; '...' = server elision, '[...]' = my joins between snippets)
new_statements.translation: [Stress in] Sungai can be predicted phonemically. This is so because stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, marked by raised pitch together with a degree of loudness. However, when the penultimate syllable contains the second vowel of a homorganic vowel cluster, the stress moves to the third syllable [from the end]. [...] Monosyllabic words are rare in Sungai but do carry stress. [...] ... stress often changes its position because the items to be emphasised are given stress. In Sungai, word emphasis often occurs on the final syllable in the phrase.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (King 1993: 'Stress is noncontrastive', ~45 penult-stressed transcriptions) on type and placement: predictable, penultimate. Refines it with (a) the identical-vowel-sequence exception (antepenultimate counting vowels separately, equivalent to stress on a long penultimate nucleus), (b) phonetic correlates (raised pitch + loudness), (c) a phrase-level statement that emphasis tends to sit on the phrase-final syllable. The phrase-final remark is explicitly 'dalam frasa' (in the phrase) and about 'penekanan' (emphasis), so it is not read as a competing word-stress rule; a full-page read (HathiTrust/print) should confirm the table's stress marks. Variety: the author…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, realised as raised pitch plus loudness; when the penult is the second half of a like-vowel sequence (e.g. the second a of aa), stress goes to the third-from-last syllable, i.e. onto the first half of the long vowel; monosyllables are rare but stressed; a table gives 2- to 5-syllable examples (a-ma, no-ra-tu, no-ko-san-tak, mi-no-mon-ti-an, pi-no-ki-tu-lung-an; stress marks lost in scanned). At phrase level, emphasis is often placed on the phrase-final syllable and stress position can shift under emphasis; intonation ('Nada') is treated separately with four pitch contours.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing on secondary stress in the snippets seen
new_statements.exceptions: (1) penult containing the second vowel of a homorganic (identical) vowel cluster -> stress on the third syllable from the end; (2) phrase-level emphasis often on the final syllable of the phrase, and stress position may shift for emphasis; (3) monosyllables carry stress
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Sungai/Tombonuwo of the Labuk-Sugut (Beluran/Paitan) area, Sabah = Glottolog tomb1244 (ISO txa); King & King's data are from the Sugut river dialect (Sungai-Sungai, Lingkabau); Abdul Hamid Ahmad's 'bahasa Sungai di Sabah' is catalogued under subject 'Tombonuwo language -- Phonology' (Open Library/Michigan MARC), so it is the same language, variety unverified.

sources.note: Discourse-syntax paper (tense-aspect, connectives, NP topicalisation, front-shifted spatio-temporal references). A full-text search of the extracted text conversion (30 PDF pages, printed pp. 45-74) finds no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, pitch, prosody, intonation, syllable, phonology or phonemics; the examples carry no accent marks; the reference list cites no phonological description (only King, Julie K., forthcoming, Some fundamentals of Tombonuo verb morphology, and Smith 1984 for classification). Nothing here bears on the catalog's fixed-stress rule or its tone class.
